# p0_docker_organization (Resource)

A Docker Hub organization that P0 can grant roles in, through one of your Docker Hub connectors.

P0 never holds the organization's access token. You store it in your own secret manager, in the connector's cloud, and the connector reads it on every call. This resource tells P0 which connector acts on the organization and where the token's secret is.

**Important:** Create the token, store it and let the connector read it before you apply this resource, in an earlier apply or in the same one with this resource depending on the connector's read grant, as the example does. Creating this resource has P0 validate the install through the connector: the connector reads the secret, signs in to Docker Hub with the token, lists the organization's members and tries an invite as a dry run, which sends nothing and uses no seat. If a check fails, the apply fails with P0's message. IAM changes can take a few seconds to take effect, so if the connector is denied the secret right after it is granted, apply again.

The connector, the vault and the secret are fixed when the organization is added, so changing `id`, `connector`, `vault` or `token_secret_name` replaces the installation. To rotate the token, store the new one as a new version of the same secret, which needs no change here. If the organization is already added in P0, import it rather than creating it: P0 refuses to add an organization twice. An installation that P0 hasn't finished, such as one imported before its checks passed, plans an update, and applying it finishes the install.

**Prerequisites:**

- A Docker Hub connector, installed with `p0_docker_connector`. The token's secret must be in the connector's cloud: AWS Secrets Manager for a connector on AWS Lambda, or Google Secret Manager for one on Cloud Run. It can be in another account or project.

- An organization access token, which needs a Docker Team or Business plan. In Docker Home, open the organization, go to **Identity & auth**, then **Access tokens**, and generate a token with the organization scopes **Member Edit** and **Invite Edit**, and no repository scopes. Store it as a secret in the account and region, or the project, that `vault` names, outside Terraform, which keeps the token out of Terraform's state.

- Read access to that one secret for the connector's identity, the connector's `connector_identity`, and to no other secret. P0 names the secret in each call, so any other secret the connector can read is one a call could point it at.

  On AWS, give the connector's role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `arn:aws:secretsmanager:<secrets_region>:<account_id>:secret:<name>-??????`. Secrets Manager adds a hyphen and six random characters to the name in a secret's ARN, and `??????` matches those, so the grant covers this one secret. If a customer-managed KMS key encrypts the secret, also give the role `kms:Decrypt` on that key, with the condition that `kms:ViaService` is `secretsmanager.<secrets_region>.amazonaws.com`. A secret in an account other than the connector's needs a customer-managed key, because the default `aws/secretsmanager` key can't be used from another account, and in that account the secret's resource policy and the key's policy must allow the connector's role too.

  On Google Cloud, give the connector's service account `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` and `roles/secretmanager.viewer` on the secret itself, not on its project.

- P0's secret manager integration for where the secret is: AWS Secrets Manager (`p0_aws_secrets_manager`) for the AWS account, or Google Secret Manager for the Google Cloud project.

**Note:** This integration is currently in beta.

For the full install steps, see [Docker Hub](https://docs.p0.dev/integrations/resource-integrations/docker).

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Adds the Docker Hub organization my-docker-org, whose organization access
# token is in AWS Secrets Manager, in the account of the connector on AWS Lambda
# that the p0_docker_connector example installs. For a connector on Cloud Run
# and a token in Google Secret Manager, see gcp.tf in this directory.
#
# Before you apply this, create the organization access token and store it as
# the secret docker/my-docker-org/token. In Docker Home, open the organization,
# go to Identity & auth, then Access tokens, and generate a token with the
# organization scopes Member Edit and Invite Edit, and no repository scopes.
# Organization access tokens need a Docker Team or Business plan. The example
# doesn't create the secret, which keeps the token out of Terraform's state.
#
# Creating p0_docker_organization has the connector read the token, so the
# token must be in its secret by then. To store it, with the AWS CLI signed in
# to the secret's account, read the token without showing it:
#
#   read -rs DOCKER_TOKEN
#
# Then create the secret:
#
#   printf %s "$DOCKER_TOKEN" | aws secretsmanager create-secret \
#     --name docker/my-docker-org/token \
#     --secret-string file:///dev/stdin --region us-west-2
#
# If the secret exists, store the token as a new version instead, which is also
# how to rotate it:
#
#   printf %s "$DOCKER_TOKEN" | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
#     --secret-id docker/my-docker-org/token \
#     --secret-string file:///dev/stdin --region us-west-2
#
# The grant is what P0's Docker Hub installer generates for the organization,
# with p0_docker_organization after it.

locals {
  p0_docker_org_my_docker_org = {
    # The connector's AWS account, which its role is in.
    connector_account_id = "123456789012"
    # The secret that holds my-docker-org's access token: its name, and the
    # account and region it's in. P0 has the connector read the secret by this
    # name there. A new secret replaces the installation. To rotate the token,
    # add a new version to this secret instead.
    token_secret_name  = "docker/my-docker-org/token"
    secrets_account_id = "123456789012"
    secrets_region     = "us-west-2"
    # The ARN of the KMS key that encrypts the secret, if that's a
    # customer-managed key. The default aws/secretsmanager key needs nothing
    # for a secret in the connector's account, but can't be used from another
    # one. For a secret in another account, set this to its customer-managed
    # key, and in that account allow the connector's role
    # secretsmanager:GetSecretValue in the secret's resource policy and
    # kms:Decrypt through Secrets Manager in the key's policy.
    kms_key_arn = null
  }
}

# IAM is global, so the region only has to be one you use. Add the credential
# settings your other AWS providers use, such as profile or assume_role, if
# they have any.
provider "aws" {
  alias               = "p0_docker_org_my_docker_org"
  region              = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_region
  allowed_account_ids = [local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.connector_account_id]
}

data "aws_partition" "p0_docker_org_my_docker_org" {
  provider = aws.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org
}

# The connector reads my-docker-org's access token, and no other secret. The
# policy goes on the connector's role, which P0 names in connector_identity.
# Each organization adds a policy of its own to that role, and a role's inline
# policies share a limit of 10,240 characters: past a few dozen organizations,
# deploy another connector for the rest.
resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "p0_docker_org_my_docker_org_token" {
  provider = aws.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org

  name = "ReadDockerHubToken-my-docker-org"
  role = p0_docker_connector.example.connector_identity.role_name
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = concat(
      [{
        Sid    = "ReadAccessToken"
        Effect = "Allow"
        Action = "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"
        # P0 gives the connector the secret's partial ARN: its ARN without the
        # hyphen and six random characters that end it. "??????" matches
        # those, so the connector gets this one secret and no other.
        Resource = join(":", [
          "arn:aws:secretsmanager",
          local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_region,
          local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_account_id,
          "secret",
          "${local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.token_secret_name}-??????",
        ])
      }],
      local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.kms_key_arn == null ? [] : [{
        Sid      = "DecryptAccessToken"
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = "kms:Decrypt"
        Resource = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.kms_key_arn
        Condition = {
          StringEquals = {
            "kms:ViaService" = "secretsmanager.${local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_region}.${data.aws_partition.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.dns_suffix}"
          }
        }
      }],
    )
  })

  # A secret in another account can't use the default aws/secretsmanager key.
  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_account_id == local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.connector_account_id || local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.kms_key_arn != null
      error_message = "The access token's secret is in another AWS account, so it must be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Set kms_key_arn to that key's ARN, and allow the connector's role in the secret's resource policy and in the key's policy."
    }
  }
}

# Adds the organization. Creating it has P0 validate the install through the
# connector, so it waits until the connector can read the token. IAM changes
# can take a few seconds to take effect, so if the connector is denied the
# secret, apply again.
resource "p0_docker_organization" "example" {
  id        = "my-docker-org"
  connector = p0_docker_connector.example.id

  vault = {
    type           = "aws-sm"
    account_id     = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_account_id
    secrets_region = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.secrets_region
  }
  token_secret_name = local.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org.token_secret_name

  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.p0_docker_org_my_docker_org_token]
}

# The email domains the connector acts for, as P0 read them back from it.
output "docker_allowed_domains" {
  value = p0_docker_organization.example.allowed_domains
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `connector` (String) The connector that acts on this organization: the `id` of a `p0_docker_connector` resource. Requires that connector to be installed.
- `id` (String) The organization's name on Docker Hub, as in its repositories' names: `<organization>/<repository>`
- `token_secret_name` (String) The name of the secret that holds the organization access token, such as `docker/my-docker-org/token` in AWS Secrets Manager or `docker-my-docker-org-token` in Google Secret Manager: the name alone, not the secret's ARN or its full resource name. In AWS Secrets Manager the name can't end in a hyphen and six letters or digits, like `-AbCdEf`, because Secrets Manager can't find a secret by such a name. Changing it replaces the installation. To rotate the token, store the new one as a new version of the same secret, which needs no change here.
- `vault` (Attributes) The secret manager that holds the organization access token. P0 never reads the token. Your connector does. It must be in the connector's cloud, and can be in another account or project. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--vault))

### Read-Only

- `allowed_domains` (String) The email domains the connector acts for: the `DOMAIN_ALLOW_PATTERN` it's deployed with, which P0 reads back from the connector when it checks the install. To change it, change the connector's deployment.
- `state` (String) This item's install progress in the P0 application:
	- 'stage': The item has been staged for installation
	- 'configure': The item is available to be added to P0, and may be configured
	- 'installed': The item is fully installed

<a id="nestedatt--vault"></a>
### Nested Schema for `vault`

Required:

- `type` (String) The secret manager: either `aws-sm` (AWS Secrets Manager) or `gcp-sm` (Google Secret Manager)

Optional:

- `account_id` (String) The ID of the AWS account that holds the access token's secret (in the P0 app, one of your AWS Secrets Manager installations). Required for, and only valid with, `aws-sm`.
- `project_id` (String) The ID of the Google Cloud project that holds the access token's secret (in the P0 app, one of your Google Secret Manager installations). Required for, and only valid with, `gcp-sm`.
- `secrets_region` (String) The AWS region the access token's secret is stored in, such as `us-west-2`. Required for, and only valid with, `aws-sm`.
